suggestions.quote: Not a new sum, either. In 1914 Henry Ford doubled his workers' pay to five dollars a day (c16), and wrote later that his own sales depended, in a measure, on the wages he paid (c17).

suggestions.quote: In 1865 the economist Jevons wrote that burning coal more efficiently did not cut the coal that got burned. The very contrary (c12). Cheaper means more.

keep.quote: Two economists wrote this sum down this year, Hemenway Falk and Tsoukalas: "The AI Layoff Trap" (c01). Each firm keeps the whole saving and bears only a slice of the spending it destroys; the rest lands on its rivals (c02). One model, not yet checked by other economists. Your napkin got there first.

Someone thought so. In 1930 the economist Keynes named it: technological unemployment, jobs lost because we save labour faster than we find new uses for it. A temporary phase, he called it (c07). And in about a hundred years, about now, he guessed, a fifteen-hour week (c08).

In the two economists' model the usual fixes fail: a basic income, a wage cut, new firms (c05). What can work, in that model, is a tax on the machine itself (c06). Their fix. Your dial. Still unchecked. Checked by Marco.
